games.explanation: Nobody wants to back a Royals team getting Skenes'd, which is exactly why the number got here. The read is simpler than the matchup looks: Skenes has been dramatically tougher on lefties this year, and Kansas City runs a heavily right-handed top of the order into him, with Witt and Garcia the kind of contact-forward righties who don't gift him the whiff. Sim has this as a coin-flip 4.6 to 4.7 slugfest, which fits a park playing neutral with the wind knocking down any mistakes. Getting +160 on a game the board is treating like a walkover is the entire ballgame.

Glasnow's walk rate is the tell everyone keeps ignoring because the strikeouts are loud enough to drown it out. He's issuing free passes to more than one in eight hitters this year, and that number climbs against righties, which is exactly the handedness San Francisco will run at him. The sim has this as a one-run game with Los Angeles winning barely more often than losing, yet the board is pricing it like a mismatch. At +250 on a coin flip dressed up as a blowout, you take the coin every time.

Cleveland is the better team, nobody's arguing that, but a run and a half is a lot of cushion to give up on a night the simulation sees separated by a single tally. The Athletics have quietly built a lineup that doesn't strike out much against righties, and Mason Barnett has been walking the tightrope well enough to keep games in the four-run neighborhood the park tends to enforce. Cleveland's offense outside of Ramirez isn't exactly a wrecking crew, and Kwan's contact-first profile is not the archetype that runs away with a game. Getting a hook and a half at plus-money on a coin-flip projection is the entire pitch, and -130 is a discount on that math.

Nick Pivetta gets treated like a frontline arm because he pitches for a contender, but the barrels and hard contact against him tell a very different story, and Miami has the exact right-handed thump to punish it. Stowers has been a menace against righties all year with a .395 xwOBA, and Hernandez and Conine bring the same barrel-heavy profile into a park that quietly plays up for the long ball. Petco keeps the total down, which is precisely how run-line dogs cash, and the sim sees this landing inside a run either way. Getting a hook and change back at -132 is the whole point.

The Yankees being favored by nearly two runs against a Diamondbacks lineup that quietly runs four above-average bats through the top of the order is the kind of price that assumes the pinstripes on the jersey do the hitting. Arizona has Marte and Perdomo doing real damage against right-handed pitching all year, and Rodriguez is competent enough to keep this from becoming the laugher the board is pricing in. Judge is Judge, but the rest of the New York lineup is a collection of solid-not-scary bats, and our sim lands on a one-run Arizona win rather than the blowout implied by the spread. At -154 you're paying a fair tax to turn a coin-flip underdog into a game that only needs to stay close, and the math says it will 66% of the time. Take the runs and let Judge hit his solo shot in a 5-4 game.

Glasnow's strikeout numbers are the shiny object, but the walk rate underneath them is what actually decides this game. He's been issuing free passes to right-handers at a 14.3% clip, which is how a supposed ace turns into a five-inning grind and how the Giants stay within a run despite being the lesser team on paper. The sim spits out a 5.4 to 5.1 finish, and Chavez Ravine's HR-friendly air keeps Los Angeles from ever pulling comfortably clear. Getting plus money on the underdog plus a run and a half against a starter who can't stop handing out baserunners is the whole ballgame.
